title: Weekly board-game sessions and loneliness in community-dwelling older adults: a randomised controlled trial
abstract: Background: Loneliness is common among older adults and is associated with poorer health outcomes. We tested whether a weekly facilitated board-game group reduces loneliness. Methods: 120 community-dwelling adults aged 65-89 were randomised to a twelve-week facilitated board-game group, playing Rummikub, dominoes and a modern cooperative tile-laying game, or to a waitlist control. The primary outcome was the UCLA Loneliness Scale at twelve weeks. Results: Loneliness scores fell by 4.2 points in the intervention arm versus 0.6 in controls. Conclusions: Regular face-to-face board-game play reduced self-reported loneliness.

title: Cooperation in a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma: evidence from a laboratory study
abstract: We study cooperation using a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma game played by 90 undergraduates in a computerised laboratory. The game serves as an incentivised measure of cooperative preference. Payoffs were monetary and behaviour was analysed with a random-effects model. Cooperation rates declined over rounds and were predicted by a self-report measure of social value orientation.

title: A mobile application adaptation of a classic strategy board game for cognitive training in older adults
abstract: We developed a tablet application version of a classic strategy board game and evaluated its effect on working memory in 60 adults aged 60-75 over eight weeks. All play took place on screen; no physical set was used. Participants improved on digit span relative to an active control app.

title: Chess instruction and mathematics attainment in primary schools: a cluster-randomised trial
abstract: Aim: To test whether a weekly chess curriculum improves mathematics attainment. Methods: 24 primary schools (n=1,120 pupils aged 8-10) were cluster-randomised to a thirty-week chess programme, in which pupils were taught and then played over-the-board chess, or to usual lessons. The primary outcome was a standardised mathematics test. Results: A small but significant advantage favoured the chess arm on problem-solving items.

title: Card game preferences and betting intensity among problem gamblers attending a casino
abstract: We surveyed 310 patrons of two casinos about their preferred card and table games and recorded wagering intensity across a single session. Problem Gambling Severity Index scores were associated with higher stakes on games of chance rather than skill.

title: Monte Carlo tree search with learned heuristics for a modern Euro-style board game
abstract: We present an agent that plays a modern resource-management board game using Monte Carlo tree search augmented with a learned value network. The agent was evaluated across 50,000 self-play games and against three scripted opponents. No human players were involved. Our agent achieves a 78% win rate against the strongest baseline.
journal: Proceedings of the Conference on Games

title: 'It gave me somewhere to be someone else': a qualitative study of tabletop role-playing groups for socially anxious adolescents
abstract: We conducted semi-structured interviews with 18 adolescents aged 13-17 who attended a weekly facilitated tabletop role-playing group run by a community mental health service, and with four facilitators. Sessions used pen, paper, dice and printed character sheets. Reflexive thematic analysis identified three themes: rehearsal of social risk, belonging through shared narrative, and transfer to school settings.

title: Designing for asymmetry: a framework for cooperative board game mechanics
abstract: This paper proposes a design framework for asymmetric roles in cooperative board games. We analyse the mechanics of twelve published titles and derive five design patterns. The framework is illustrated with a worked design example. No playtesting data with participants are reported here; empirical evaluation is left to future work.

title: What do care homes actually offer? A survey of activity provision in 210 residential settings
abstract: We surveyed activity coordinators in 210 residential care homes about the recreational activities offered to residents. Board games and card games were available in 84% of settings and were run at least weekly in 41%. Provision varied by home size and staffing. We did not assess resident outcomes.

title: Mahjong participation and rate of cognitive decline: an eight-year prospective cohort study
abstract: Objective: To examine whether regular mahjong play is associated with slower cognitive decline. Methods: 2,840 adults aged 60 and over were followed for eight years. Frequency of playing mahjong with physical tiles was recorded at baseline and biennially. Cognition was measured with the MMSE. Linear mixed models adjusted for education, baseline cognition and comorbidity. Results: Playing at least weekly was associated with a slower rate of MMSE decline.
